# Sharp projective energy in terms of retained mass and total volume

Let K be a compact convex body in R^d, d>=1, let y be interior, and put
V=|K|. Define

    E=E_K(y)=min_a integral_K[1+a.(x-y)]^(-d-1) dx,
    T=T_K(y)=max{integral_K rho:
                  0<=rho<=1, integral_K(x-y)rho(x)dx=0}.

The denominator in the first minimum is positive on K. Both extrema
are attained. Put tau=T/V and Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.

**Theorem.** The sharp total-volume refinement is

    E/V <= (d+1)tau-d tau^(1+1/d),                    (1)

or equivalently

    E <= (d+1)T-d T^(1+1/d)/V^(1/d).

For d=1 equality holds for every interval and interior mark. For d>=2:
if T=V, equality holds and y is the centroid of K; if T<V, equality
holds exactly for a cone over a convex (d-1)-base, with y on the
base-centroid/apex segment strictly between the centroid of K and its
apex. Affine images are included. In particular every tau in (0,1]
is attained in an equality example.

The proof retains the actual total volume in the earlier centroidal
cap comparison of `candidate 49e262af8d182671`,
Section 3. The new step truncates that comparison cone at the unique
level matching the exterior mass. The resulting inequality was
independently proposed and derived by root and research-agent.

## 1. Actual maximizing retained cap and its two moments

Translate y to zero. For completeness the convex hinge objective

    G(u)=integral_K(1+u.x)_+ dx

is finite, C1 and coercive: an inner ball centered at zero gives a lower
bound c||u||, and differentiation under the integral gives

    grad G(u)=integral_(K intersect {1+u.x>=0}) x dx.

A minimizing u_* therefore produces a convex cap
D=K intersect {1+u_*.x>=0} with centroid zero. Its volume is G(u_*).
For any feasible rho, its zero moment gives

    integral rho = integral(1+u_*.x)rho <= G(u_*)=|D|.

Thus T=|D|, attained by its actual indicator. When zero is the centroid
of K, T=V and E=V by energy stationarity. Conversely T=V forces the
maximizing indicator to be one almost everywhere and hence g_K=0.
This proves (1) and the stated equality in that case.

Assume henceforth d>=2 and T<V. Then u_* is nonzero and cuts K
properly. Use the height t=u_*.x and its coarea-normalized section
density f, so integral_K h(u_*.x)dx=integral h(t)f(t)dt. The support is
[A,B], where A<-1<0<B. The function f^(1/(d-1)) is concave on its
interior, by actual section inclusion and Brunn--Minkowski. Extend f
by zero outside its support; endpoint values are immaterial. Exactly

    integral_(-1)^B f=T,      integral_(-1)^B t f=0.  (2)

The top endpoint obeys B<=d. Indeed select a highest point of D. Its
homothety of D by ratio (B-s)/(B+1) lies in D intersect {t>=s}, for
-1<=s<=B. Therefore the survival probability of uniform D is at least
[(B-s)/(B+1)]^d. Integrating it gives

    1=E_D(t+1) >= (B+1)/(d+1).

This proves the endpoint bound even if the highest supporting face
has positive dimension.

## 2. Convex order on the retained side

Put N=d+1 and define an untruncated comparison cone density

    g(t)=(dT/N)((d-t)/N)^(d-1),     t<=d.

Its restriction to [-1,d] has mass T and first moment zero, matching
(2). On the actual support the root difference

    q(t)=f(t)^(1/(d-1))-(dT/N)^(1/(d-1))(d-t)/N

is concave. Since B<=d, the set where f-g is positive on [-1,d]
is an interval. Either f=g almost everywhere there, or that positive
interval has endpoints -1<r_1<r_2<d, with signs

    f-g:       nonpositive, positive, nonpositive.    (3)

Here are the boundary details. Matching masses forces a nonempty
positive interval unless there is equality. If its left endpoint
were -1, the sign of (t-r_2)(f-g) would be everywhere nonpositive
and strictly negative on a set of positive measure, contradicting
the two equal moments. If its right endpoint were d, the analogous
argument with (t-r_1)(f-g) would be everywhere nonnegative and
strict somewhere. A possible nonzero facet density at B simply
jumps downward to zero beyond B and does not alter the sign pattern.

For a finite convex function w on [-1,d], subtract the secant through
(r_1,w(r_1)) and (r_2,w(r_2)). The difference w-sec is nonpositive
between the endpoints and nonnegative outside. By (3),

    integral_(-1)^d w f <= integral_(-1)^d w g.        (4)

The affine secant integrates to zero against f-g by (2). For strictly
convex w, equality in (4) forces f=g almost everywhere on this side.

The same concavity also proves

    f(t)<=g(t) for all t<-1, up to endpoint values.    (5)

In the unequal case q(-1)<=0 and q(s)>0 at some s>-1.
Concavity at -1 between t<-1 and s then forces q(t)<0. In the equal
case, q is zero on the retained interior; concavity with two such
points forces q(t)<=0 on the left. Outside the actual support f=0.

## 3. Matching total volume on the exterior side

Let eta=tau^(1/d), and choose

    a=d-N/eta < -1,
    psi(t)=g(t) for a<=t<=d, and zero otherwise.

Direct integration gives

    integral psi = T((d-a)/N)^d = V.

Thus f and psi have the same exterior mass V-T below -1. For t<a
their difference is nonnegative, while for a<t<-1 it is nonpositive
by (5). For every increasing w finite on the actual and comparison
supports, the one-crossing rule gives

    integral_(t<-1) w f <= integral_(t<-1) w psi.      (6)

To verify it subtract w(a); the product (f-psi)(w-w(a)) is nonpositive
on both sides and the exterior masses match. If w is strictly
increasing, equality requires f=psi almost everywhere below -1.
The actual body may extend farther left than a; that creates no
admissibility or sign problem.

## 4. The admissible increasing convex energy kernel

Set

    c=(eta-1)/(N-d eta)<0,     w(t)=(1+c t)^(-N).

The endpoint denominators of the comparison cone are

    1+c d=1/(N-d eta),        1+c a=1/eta.             (7)

Since c<0 and the actual top B<=d, this denominator is positive on
ALL of K; farther-negative actual points only increase it. The
function w is strictly increasing and strictly convex there. It is
an admissible physical projective parameter c u_*. Combining (4)
and (6),

    E <= integral f w <= integral psi w.              (8)

For a cone density on [a,d], normalized by its total mass V, the
elementary integral identity is

    (1/V) integral psi(t)(1+c t)^(-d-1)dt
      =1/[(1+c d)(1+c a)^d].

For example, substitute s=(d-t)/(d-a) and differentiate
s^d/[L_d(L_d+(L_a-L_d)s)^d], with L_d=1+c d, L_a=1+c a.
Using (7), the right side becomes

    (N-d eta)eta^d=(d+1)tau-d tau^(1+1/d).

This proves (1) for every proper retained cap, without choosing an
optimal direction for ordinary halfspace depth.

## 5. Equality and the one-dimensional case

Suppose d>=2 and T<V. Both comparisons in (8) have nonnegative
deficits. Strict convexity on the retained side and strict increase
on the exterior side show that equality implies f=psi almost
everywhere on the whole line.

This section profile forces the actual K to be a cone. Sections
converge in Hausdorff distance to an endpoint section: the upper
inclusion follows from compactness, and the lower inclusion by
interpolation with a fixed interior point. Thus its bottom section
at a has the prescribed positive (d-1)-volume. Choose a top point
at d. Its cone over this bottom section lies in K and has exactly
the same section volumes as K at every interior height. Included
positive convex sections with equal volume are equal. Closure
identifies K with this cone and forces its top to be a single point.

The retained cap D is then the homothetic apex subcone cut at -1.
Its actual centroid is y=0 by construction, so y lies on the axis
from the full base centroid to the apex. Since the full base lies
strictly below -1, y lies strictly between g_K and the apex.

Conversely, in any such cone and axial mark, the apex subcone with
centroid y is an actual cap. Its indicator is the maximal retained
mass by the hinge argument in Section 1. Its section density is
exactly psi after normalizing its cut to -1, and the parameter in
Section 4 is fully stationary: section centroids lie on the axis,
while its one-dimensional weighted moment vanishes. Hence it is
the unique full projective optimizer and equality holds. Equivalently
one may use the exact cone energy formula from
`candidate 5f5575d4f9e40719`.

For d=1 write K=[-l,r], l,r>0. Directly

    V=l+r,    T=2 min(l,r),    E=4lr/(l+r).

Consequently E/V=2tau-tau^2, exactly (1). This covers every interval
and every interior mark, including the midpoint case tau=1.

## 6. Exact domination of the inverse-energy depth certificate

Recall the strictly increasing function on [0,Gamma_d]

    F_d(alpha)=((d+1)^(d+1)/d^d)alpha(1-alpha^(1/d)).

An exact substitution yields

    F_d(Gamma_d tau)=(d+1)tau-d tau^(1+1/d).

Thus (1) is equivalent to

    V F_d^(-1)(E/V) <= Gamma_d T_K(y).                (9)

The right side is a valid ordinary cap guarantee: retain the actual
centroidal cap D and apply the ordinary centroid theorem to D.
Furthermore T^(1/d) is jointly Minkowski-concave, including arbitrary
containing target fibers, as proved in
`candidate 38e8cdfda56d1d3d`.

Therefore the sharp inverse-energy OWN-FIBER depth certificate never
improves the already available physical retained-mass guarantee.
Equality is exactly as classified above. This explains the scalar
anchored-mixing failure in
`candidate 3208a2842914cf02`:
the inverse-energy certificate can decrease under inclusion whereas
the physical retained mass cannot.

This domination is a stopping rule for that proposed scalar bridge.
It does not compare every directional energy/cap estimate with every
possible coupled-fiber argument, and it does not prove OC or a new
integer-base allocation theorem.
